mcqs.question: An image is purely decorative. What is the correct way to keep it out of screen-reader output?
options: Give it role="img" and no alt attribute
mcqs.explanation: An intentionally empty alt tells assistive technology the image is decorative and can be skipped. The strongest distractor is option 0: a missing alt is not the same statement; it is unspecified, and screen readers may announce the filename or the image's presence, forcing users to guess. Option 1 announces the literal words 'decorative image', and option 3 creates an image with no name at all.

mcqs.question: A teammate adds maximum-scale=1, user-scalable=no to the viewport meta to stop unwanted zoom. What is the impact?
options: It is fine as long as desktop users can still zoom with browser controls
It improves accessibility by preventing accidental zoom
It can prevent pinch-zoom and text resizing, removing a primary low-vision strategy and conflicting with WCAG resize-text requirements
Browsers universally ignore it, so there is no effect
mcqs.explanation: Zoom is part of the accessible responsive experience, and blocking it takes away how many low-vision users read the page, conflicting with the ability to resize text. The usual motivation, iOS zooming into focused inputs, is better solved by giving inputs a 16px font size (https://css-tricks.com/16px-or-larger-text-prevents-ios-form-zoom). The strongest distractor is option 3: some modern browsers ignore the flag in some conditions, but plenty of browser and WebView combinations still honor it, so 'universally ignored' is false and dangerous.

mcqs.question: A page has a header navigation, a breadcrumb, and a footer navigation, all marked up as nav. How do you make them distinguishable for screen-reader users?
options: Give each repeated nav a distinguishing label, for example aria-label="Primary", "Breadcrumb", and "Footer"
Replace two of them with div elements so only one nav remains
Rely on the links inside each nav to explain the difference
Add an h2 inside each nav so the heading structure distinguishes them
mcqs.explanation: Repeated landmarks of the same type should carry distinguishing labels so the landmark list shows three different entries and users can jump straight to the one they need. The strongest distractor is option 1: removing nav semantics throws away free navigation structure instead of disambiguating it. Option 3 is a real half-measure: headings help heading-based navigation but do not label the landmarks themselves.

scenarios.prompt: At widths of 60rem and up, this page renders visually as Filters on the left, then Results, then Details. Describe exactly what (a) a screen-reader user reading linearly and (b) a keyboard-only user experience at that width, why it happens, and how you would fix it without changing the visual design.

code.code:
Result 1

Details

scenarios.modelAnswer: The DOM order is Results, Details, Filters, and neither screen-reader reading order nor sequential keyboard navigation follows grid placement; both follow the document. So at desktop widths a screen-reader user hears the results first, then the details, then finally the filters that scope them, and a keyboard user tabs into Result 1 before ever reaching the filter checkbox. Sighted users see Filters first, which is presumably the intended task flow, so the two audiences get different sequences and focus appears to jump around when compared with the visual layout. The fix is not CSS trickery and never positive tabindex: reorder the HTML source so the logical order is Filters, Results, Details, and keep the grid placement purely as the visual presentation of that order. Then test by reading the page and tabbing through every interactive element at each responsive layout, because the narrow layout must also make sense in the new source order.
rubric: States that reading order and tab order follow DOM source order, not grid-template-areas placement.
Describes the concrete mismatch: users hit Results and Details before the Filters that scope them.
Fixes the HTML source order and keeps grid placement as presentation only.
Rejects positive tabindex as a patch and can explain why (separate order, maintenance burden, does not fix reading order).
Mentions re-testing keyboard traversal and reading order at every breakpoint, including the narrow layout.
